title: What manual handling training is required under EU law?
description: What Article 6 of Directive 90/269/EEC requires for manual handling information and training, load weight data, and the Annex risk factors to cover.
shortAnswer: The EU Manual Handling Directive (Council Directive 90/269/EEC) requires employers to give workers proper training and information on how to handle loads correctly and on the risks of doing it incorrectly, having regard to the load, effort, environment, activity, and individual risk factors in Annexes I and II. Article 6 also requires information on the weight of a load and, for eccentric loads, the center of gravity of the heaviest side. Training supplements, never replaces, avoiding manual handling.
keyTakeaways: Article 6(2) of Directive 90/269/EEC requires proper training and information on how to handle loads correctly and the risks of incorrect handling.
Article 6(1) requires general indications and, where possible, precise information on load weight and the center of gravity of the heaviest side of an eccentrically loaded package.
Training must take account of the four Annex I reference factors and the Annex II individual factors, one of which is a worker lacking adequate knowledge or training.
Training is the last step in a hierarchy: Article 3 first requires avoiding manual handling, then reducing its risk through organization and mechanical aids.
The directive sets no maximum weight and no training interval; national laws transposing it may add both.
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National labor inspectorates enforce the transposing laws; the European Commission monitors transposition; the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) publishes guidance
appliesTo: Employers whose workers lift, put down, push, pull, carry, move, or support loads
Workers in logistics, retail, construction, manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare patient handling
Supervisors who organize workstations and set work rates
Workers' representatives with a safety and health role

sections.heading: What is the EU Manual Handling Directive?

blocks.text: The Manual Handling Directive is [Council Directive 90/269/EEC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:01990L0269-20190726) of May 29, 1990, which sets minimum health and safety requirements for the manual handling of loads "where there is a risk particularly of back injury to workers". It is the fourth individual directive under the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), and Article 1(2) applies the Framework Directive fully alongside it. Member States had to transpose it by December 31, 1992 (Article 9).

Article 2 defines manual handling of loads as "any transporting or supporting of a load, by one or more workers, including lifting, putting down, pushing, pulling, carrying or moving of a load, which, by reason of its characteristics or of unfavourable ergonomic conditions, involves a risk particularly of back injury to workers". The definition includes pushing and pulling, team lifts, and static support, not only lifting. As at November 2026, the consolidated text dated July 26, 2019 is current.

sections.heading: Where does training fit in the employer's duties?

blocks.text: Training is the final layer of a hierarchy, not the first response. Article 3(1) requires the employer to take appropriate organizational measures, or use appropriate means, "in particular mechanical equipment", to avoid the need for workers to handle loads manually at all.

Where manual handling cannot be avoided, Article 3(2) requires measures to reduce the risk, and Article 4 requires the employer to organize workstations so that handling is as safe and healthy as possible and to "assess, in advance if possible" the health and safety conditions of the work, examining the characteristics of the loads. A training program that teaches lifting technique while ignoring a load that should have been mechanized will not satisfy the directive, and it is a common finding in incident investigations.

sections.heading: What does Article 6 require for information and training?

blocks.text: Article 6 has two parts: information on the measures and the loads, and training on correct handling and its risks. Both sit on top of the Framework Directive's general duties.

Under Article 6(1), workers and/or their representatives must be informed of all measures implemented under the directive. Employers must also ensure that workers receive "general indications and, where possible, precise information on" two things: the weight of a load, and the center of gravity of the heaviest side when a package is eccentrically loaded. In practice that means weight marking or weight data at the point of handling, not only in the training room.

Article 6(2) requires that employers "ensure that workers receive in addition proper training and information on how to handle loads correctly and the risks they might be open to particularly if these tasks are not performed correctly, having regard to Annexes I and II".

blocks.title: A drafting error in the official text
blocks.text: In the Official Journal version of Article 6(2), the cross reference reads "Article 12 of Directive 83/391/EEC". The context, and Article 6(1), which refers to Article 10 of Directive 89/391/EEC, show that the Framework Directive 89/391/EEC is meant. The error also appears in the consolidated text, so citations in training documentation should use 89/391/EEC.

sections.heading: Which risk factors must the training cover?

blocks.text: Training must be designed "having regard to" the risk factors in Annexes I and II, so the content should teach workers to recognize each factor in their own tasks. The annexes are reference lists for a multi factor analysis, and EU-OSHA's [summary of Directive 90/269/EEC](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directives/6) lists them in the same four plus one structure.

blocks.caption: Annex I and II risk factors and how a training program can address them
head: Annex factor
Examples given in the directive
What training should enable the worker to do
rows: Annex I(1): characteristics of the load
Too heavy or too large, unwieldy, unstable or shifting contents, held away from the trunk or with bending or twisting
Read weight and center of gravity information, test a load, and decide when to use a mechanical aid or a team lift
Annex I(2): physical effort required
Too strenuous, only achieved by twisting the trunk, likely to cause sudden load movement, unstable posture
Plan the move, position feet, and avoid twisting by turning the whole body
Annex I(3): working environment
Not enough room, uneven or slippery floor, unsafe height, changes in level, unstable floor, unsuitable temperature, humidity or ventilation
Check the route and the destination, and report environment defects before handling
Annex I(4): requirements of the activity
Over frequent or prolonged effort, insufficient rest or recovery, excessive distances, rate of work imposed by a process the worker cannot alter
Use rest and rotation arrangements and report unsustainable work rates
Annex II: individual risk factors
Physically unsuited to the task, unsuitable clothing or footwear, inadequate or inappropriate knowledge or training
Recognize personal limits, wear suitable footwear, and request instruction before an unfamiliar task

blocks.text: Annex II is notable because it names lack of "adequate or appropriate knowledge or training" as a risk factor in itself. Article 5 requires Annex II to be taken into account when the Framework Directive's rules on assigning tasks to workers and on health surveillance are applied, which links capability decisions to training records.

sections.heading: What evidence would an inspector expect?

blocks.text: An inspector will look for a link between the assessed tasks, the controls chosen, and training that reflects those specific tasks. The table maps each obligation to role, frequency, and evidence.

blocks.text: A practical assessment is stronger evidence than attendance alone, because the directive asks for training on handling loads "correctly". The difference is discussed in [completion tracking vs competency verification](/compare/completion-tracking-vs-competency-verification), and a defensible refresh cycle can be set using [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What does the directive leave to national law?

blocks.text: The directive sets no maximum load weight, no minimum training hours, and no retraining interval. Those details, where they exist, come from each Member State's transposing law, national guidance, or harmonized standards that national authorities reference.

Because the directive is a minimum, a training program for a multinational should use the directive's structure (avoid, assess, reduce, inform, train) as a common core and add national rules country by country, following [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations). Office based handling sits beside the [display screen equipment directive](/regulations/eu-display-screen-equipment-directive-training), and both were covered in the Commission's communication on practical implementation that EU-OSHA links from its summary.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each handling task with its Annex I and II factors, controls, and practical assessment points, linked to the roles that perform it. When a load, route, or piece of equipment changes, the affected tasks and the workers who need retraining can be identified from those links.

faqs.q: Does EU law set a maximum weight a worker can lift?
faqs.a: Not in Directive 90/269/EEC. The directive uses a risk based approach built on the Annex I and II factors rather than a single weight limit. Some Member States set reference weights or limits in national law or guidance, so the transposing law should be checked.

faqs.q: Is a generic lifting technique video enough to comply?
faqs.a: Unlikely on its own. Article 6(2) requires training on handling loads correctly and on the risks, having regard to the Annex factors, which vary by task. Training should reflect the worker's actual loads, environment, and equipment, ideally with a practical check.

faqs.q: Does the directive apply to pushing trolleys or moving patients?
faqs.a: Yes, where there is a risk particularly of back injury. Article 2 covers pushing, pulling, carrying, moving and supporting a load, by one or more workers. Patient handling and trolley work are therefore within scope when their characteristics or the ergonomic conditions create that risk.
